pages.title: Turn a big task into small steps

elements.name: lai.ai-you-can-use.l12.intro
elements.html:
Design a workflow with checkpoints and proportionate resource use.

Break a task into a goal, inputs, draft, checks and a human decision. Use the simplest method that does the job well. AI services use computing infrastructure; electricity and water impacts vary with model, task, hardware, power supply and cooling. Training and repeated use both matter, and wider benefits or harms depend on the application. A fixed universal water-per-prompt number hides these differences. Compare options honestly without pretending you can calculate an exact footprint from a chat counter.

Practice scenario

Fictional task: produce a one-page club guide. You already have verified rules. Options: edit a template, request one text outline, or produce a short animated guide. Compare the options with the same audience and task; do not assume extra media is necessary.

choices.text: Set goal → use permitted facts → draft → check facts/accessibility → approve.
Draft → polish the wording → publish, without checking the source facts.
Generate endlessly until something feels right.

choices.text: Every AI message uses exactly the same amount of water.
Use the template or a limited text draft if useful; avoid needless media and state that exact impact is unknown.
Digital work has no physical resource costs.

elements.title: Draw or describe a five-step workflow for the guide. Name a non-AI option, a stopping rule, and what information you would need for a fair environmental comparison.
elements.description: Practice text only. Saved on this device. Reviewed by you or an educator, not AI graded.

validators.text: Add enough reasoning to review (at least 30 characters).

elements.name: lai.ai-you-can-use.l12.rubric
elements.html:
Self-check

  • Includes a factual check and human approval.
  • Uses a proportionate method and stopping rule.
  • Names relevant footprint uncertainty rather than a universal rate.

IEA figures are aggregate estimates/projections; the water paper models particular cases. Neither gives a universal measured footprint for your prompt.
